claim: C. crescentus is a monopolarly flagellated alpha-proteobacterium.
source: Here we reconstitute and dissect the substrate specificity underpinning the cytoplasmic O-glycosylation pathway that modifies all six flagellins, five structural and one regulatory paralog, in Caulobacter crescentus, a monopolarly flagellated alpha-proteobacterium.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of the organism.

claim: C. crescentus has six flagellin paralogs: five structural and one regulatory.
source: Here we reconstitute and dissect the substrate specificity underpinning the cytoplasmic O-glycosylation pathway that modifies all six flagellins, five structural and one regulatory paralog, in Caulobacter crescentus, a monopolarly flagellated alpha-proteobacterium.

claim: The pseudaminic acid biosynthetic pathway is required for flagellation in C. crescentus.
source: We characterize the biosynthetic pathway for the sialic acid-like sugar pseudaminic acid and show its requirement for flagellation, flagellin modification and efficient export.

source: The cognate NeuB enzyme that condenses phosphoenolpyruvate with a hexose into pseudaminic acid is functionally interchangeable with other pseudaminic acid synthases.

source: FlmG accumulates before the FlaF secretion chaperone, potentially timing flagellin modification, export, and assembly during the cell division cycle.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this temporal relationship.

claim: The temporal accumulation of FlmG before FlaF potentially times flagellin modification, export, and assembly during the cell division cycle.
source: FlmG accumulates before the FlaF secretion chaperone, potentially timing flagellin modification, export, and assembly during the cell division cycle.
evidence: The abstract suggests this as a potential mechanism.

claim: Bacterial extracellular proteinaceous surface structures including pili, flagella, and autotransporters as well as toxins are often post-translationally modified by glycosylation.
source: In bacteria, extracellular proteinaceous surface structures including pili, flagella, and autotransporters as well as toxins are often post-translationally modified by glycosylation (Nothaft and Szymanski, 2010; Valguarnera et al., 2016; Vimr et al., 2004; De Maayer and Cowan, 2016; Miller et al., 2008; Szymanski et al., 2003; Schäffer and Messner, 2017; Goon et al., 2003; Schirm et al., 2003; Shen et al., 2006; Sulzenbacher et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Glycosylation of pili and flagella is often linked to virulence and evasion from the host immune system by molecular mimicry.
source: Since pili and flagella may be exposed to immune surveillance systems of eukaryotic cells, glycosylation of the structural subunits of these appendages, the pilin or flagellin, is often linked to virulence and evasion from the host immune system by molecular mimicry (Nothaft and Szymanski, 2010; Schäffer and Messner, 2017; Arora et al., 2005; Logan, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Flagellin methylation in Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium promotes adhesion to host cells.
source: In Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium another type of flagellin modification, methylation, was recently shown to promote adhesion to host cells (Horstmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Glycosylation systems are not restricted to pathogens but also occur in non-pathogenic bacteria found in the environment.
source: Flagellin glycosylation may potentially affect flagellar motility in many bacterial lineages since genomic and mass spectrometry data reveal that glycosylation systems are not restricted to pathogens but also occur in non-pathogenic bacteria found in the environment (De Maayer and Cowan, 2016; Schirm et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: In several polarly flagellated Gram-negative bacteria, flagellin glycosylation is required for assembly of the flagellar filament.
source: In several polarly flagellated Gram-negative bacteria, flagellin glycosylation is required for assembly of the flagellar filament.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation in the introduction.

claim: In Campylobacter jejuni and Helicobacter pylori, glycosylation is required for flagellar assembly, motility, and virulence.
source: In Campylobacter jejuni and Helicobacter pylori, two epsilon-proteobacteria that cause a broad range of human and animal diseases, glycosylation is required for flagellar assembly, motility, and virulence (Schirm et al., 2003; Linton et al., 2000; Guerry et al., 2006; Zebian et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: H. pylori has a monopolar flagellum.
source: H. pylori has a monopolar flagellum, while C. jejuni is bipolarly flagellated (Kostrzynska et al., 1991; Guerry et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: C. jejuni is bipolarly flagellated.
source: H. pylori has a monopolar flagellum, while C. jejuni is bipolarly flagellated (Kostrzynska et al., 1991; Guerry et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: In Campylobacter species, a nine-carbon sugar related to sialic acids such as a pseudaminic acid or legionaminic acid derivative is appended to the flagellin.
source: In Campylobacter species, the exact chemical nature of glycosylation is variable but generally a nine-carbon sugar related to sialic acids such as a pseudaminic acid or legionaminic acid derivative is appended to the flagellin (Thibault et al., 2001; Logan et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Many Campylobacter strains possess three dedicated NeuB-like synthases: one for sialic acid, one for legionaminic acid, and one for pseudaminic acid.
source: Many Campylobacter strains possess three dedicated NeuB-like synthases: one for sialic acid (incorporated into the lipo-oligosaccharide), one for legionaminic acid, and one for pseudaminic acid, both used to modify flagellins (Linton et al., 2000; Sundaram et al., 2004; Chou et al., 2005; McNally et al., 2006; McNally et al., 2007; Schoenhofen et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Helicobacter species use pseudaminic acid only for flagellin glycosylation.
source: By contrast, Helicobacter species seem to use pseudaminic acid only for flagellin glycosylation (McNally et al., 2006; McNally et al., 2007; Schoenhofen et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: In both C. jejuni and H. pylori, loss of pseudaminic acid biosynthesis results in non-motile strains lacking flagella.
source: In both C. jejuni and H. pylori, loss of pseudaminic acid biosynthesis results in non-motile strains lacking flagella.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous studies.

claim: The abundance of intracellular flagellin is severely reduced in C. jejuni and H. pylori mutants lacking pseudaminic acid biosynthesis.
source: The abundance of intracellular flagellin is severely reduced in these mutants and the flagellins showed increased mobility by SDS-PAGE (polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis), consistent with the loss of glycosylation (Schirm et al., 2003; Linton et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Flagellins in C. jejuni and H. pylori mutants lacking pseudaminic acid biosynthesis show increased mobility by SDS-PAGE, consistent with the loss of glycosylation.
source: The abundance of intracellular flagellin is severely reduced in these mutants and the flagellins showed increased mobility by SDS-PAGE (polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis), consistent with the loss of glycosylation (Schirm et al., 2003; Linton et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Polar flagellation in pathogenic Aeromonas spp and Shewanella oneidensis depends on glycosylation of flagellin with pseudaminic acid and another nonulosonic acid derivative, respectively.
source: Similarly, polar flagellation in the gamma-proteobacteria such as pathogenic Aeromonas spp and the non-pathogenic environmental bacterium Shewanella oneidensis depends on glycosylation of flagellin with pseudaminic acid and another nonulosonic acid derivative, respectively (Sun et al., 2013; Schirm et al., 2005; Wilhelms et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Pseudaminic acid is a component of surface polysaccharides such as the O-antigen of lipopolysaccharide in Aeromonas caviae.
source: Interestingly, pseudaminic acid is also a component of surface polysaccharides such as the O-antigen of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in Aeromonas caviae or the capsular polysaccharide (K antigen) in the symbiotic alpha-proteobacterium Sinorhizobium fredii NGR234 (Forsberg and Reuhs, 1997; Le Quéré et al., 2006; Margaret et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Pseudaminic acid is a component of the capsular polysaccharide (K antigen) in Sinorhizobium fredii NGR234.
source: Interestingly, pseudaminic acid is also a component of surface polysaccharides such as the O-antigen of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in Aeromonas caviae or the capsular polysaccharide (K antigen) in the symbiotic alpha-proteobacterium Sinorhizobium fredii NGR234 (Forsberg and Reuhs, 1997; Le Quéré et al., 2006; Margaret et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: In A. caviae, the genes required for pseudaminic acid biosynthesis are encoded in the O-antigen cluster and their mutation affects both flagellum and LPS O-antigen biosynthesis.
source: In A. caviae, the genes required for pseudaminic acid biosynthesis are encoded in the O-antigen cluster and their mutation affects both flagellum and LPS O-antigen biosynthesis (Canals et al., 2007; Tabei et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Flagellin glycosylation occurs at serine or threonine residues by O-linking glycosyltransferases.
source: Flagellin glycosylation occurs at serine or threonine residues by O-linking glycosyltransferases (henceforth OGTs) that modify their substrates to various extent for each flagellin system, ranging from modification at a single site for Burkholderia and Listeria species (Shen et al., 2006; Scott et al., 2011; Hanuszkiewicz et al., 2014) to promiscuous modification at 19 serine or threonine residues for the C. jejuni flagellin (Schirm et al., 2005; Thibault et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Flagellin glycosylation ranges from modification at a single site for Burkholderia and Listeria species to promiscuous modification at 19 serine or threonine residues for the C. jejuni flagellin.
source: Flagellin glycosylation occurs at serine or threonine residues by O-linking glycosyltransferases (henceforth OGTs) that modify their substrates to various extent for each flagellin system, ranging from modification at a single site for Burkholderia and Listeria species (Shen et al., 2006; Scott et al., 2011; Hanuszkiewicz et al., 2014) to promiscuous modification at 19 serine or threonine residues for the C. jejuni flagellin (Schirm et al., 2005; Thibault et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The modification by glycosylation usually occurs at the two surface-exposed central domains of flagellin.
source: The modification usually occurs at the two surface-exposed central domains of flagellin, ideally positioned to influence the immunogenicity of the filament and the virulence in pathogens (Arora et al., 2005; Verma et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: No consensus sequence determinant in the primary structure of the flagellin acceptor (apart from the serine or threonine modification site) has been identified.
source: Since no consensus sequence determinant in the primary structure of the flagellin acceptor (apart from the serine or threonine modification site) has been identified (Thibault et al., 2001), OGTs likely recognize the tertiary structure of the glycosyl acceptor in a highly specific manner.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: OGTs likely recognize the tertiary structure of the glycosyl acceptor in a highly specific manner.
source: Since no consensus sequence determinant in the primary structure of the flagellin acceptor (apart from the serine or threonine modification site) has been identified (Thibault et al., 2001), OGTs likely recognize the tertiary structure of the glycosyl acceptor in a highly specific manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of consensus sequence.

claim: Evidence has been provided that glycosylation precedes secretion of the flagellin.
source: Evidence has been provided that glycosylation precedes secretion of the flagellin (Parker et al., 2014) via the flagellar export machinery to the tip of the growing flagellar filament (Chevance and Hughes, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Flagellin identification and subsequent glycosylation by the OGT must occur in the cytoplasm.
source: Thus, flagellin identification and subsequent glycosylation by the OGT must occur in the cytoplasm, presumably by soluble proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of glycosylation before secretion.

claim: During flagellar assembly in Gram-negative bacteria, the basal body harboring the export apparatus is assembled first in the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: During flagellar assembly in Gram-negative (diderm) bacteria, the basal body harboring the export apparatus is assembled first in the cytoplasmic membrane, followed by envelope-spanning structures along with the external hook structure that serves as universal joint between the flagellar filament and the envelope-spanning parts (Chevance and Hughes, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The flagellins are assembled last by polymerization on the hook into the flagellar filament.
source: The flagellins are assembled last by polymerization on the hook into the flagellar filament (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Flagellins are usually the last proteins to be expressed and secreted during flagellar assembly.
source: They are usually the last proteins to be expressed and secreted during assembly, relying on temporal control mechanisms of gene expression promoting the orderly assembly of the flagellum.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle of flagellar assembly.

claim: Polarly or bipolarly flagellated bacteria must assemble a new flagellum each cell cycle.
source: A key feature of polarly or bipolarly flagellated bacteria is that they must assemble a new flagellum each cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of these bacteria.

claim: C. crescentus serves as a model system to study how flagellation is regulated in space and as a function of the cell cycle.
source: The non-pathogenic and polarized alpha-proteobacterium C. crescentus serves as a model system to study how flagellation is regulated in space and as a function of the cell cycle (Skerker and Laub, 2004; Ardissone and Viollier, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: C. crescentus assembles a single flagellum at the newborn cell pole each cell cycle.
source: C. crescentus assembles a single flagellum at the newborn cell pole each cell cycle and then divides asymmetrically into a flagellated but non-replicative dispersal (swarmer, SW) cell that resides in a G1-like phase, and a capsulated sessile (stalked, ST) cell that engages in DNA synthesis (S-phase) and harbors the defining stalked appendage at the old cell pole (Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement describes the cell cycle of C. crescentus and references Figure 1B.

claim: C. crescentus divides asymmetrically into a flagellated swarmer cell and a capsulated stalked cell.
source: C. crescentus assembles a single flagellum at the newborn cell pole each cell cycle and then divides asymmetrically into a flagellated but non-replicative dispersal (swarmer, SW) cell that resides in a G1-like phase, and a capsulated sessile (stalked, ST) cell that engages in DNA synthesis (S-phase) and harbors the defining stalked appendage at the old cell pole (Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement describes the cell cycle of C. crescentus and references Figure 1B.

claim: Each C. crescentus swarmer cell undergoes a metamorphosis into a stalked cell, replacing the flagellum with a stalk.
source: Each SW cell undergoes a metamorphosis into a ST cell, replacing the flagellum with a stalk, a cylindrical extension of the cell envelope.
evidence: This statement describes the cell cycle transition in C. crescentus.

claim: The flagellar filament and hook are released during the SW to ST cell transition in C. crescentus.
source: In doing so, the flagellar filament and hook are released during the SW to ST cell transition while stalk outgrowth commences.
evidence: This statement describes events during the cell cycle transition.

claim: Multiple spatiotemporal cell cycle control mechanisms feed into flagellar assembly in C. crescentus.
source: Multiple spatiotemporal cell cycle control mechanisms feed into flagellar assembly in C. crescentus (Ardissone and Viollier, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Spatial cues that direct assembly of the flagellum to the proper site are deposited during cell division in the preceding cell cycle and inherited by the progeny.
source: First, spatial cues that direct assembly of the flagellum to the proper site are deposited during cell division in the preceding cell cycle and inherited by the progeny (Huitema et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: In S-phase, the transcriptional cell cycle activator CtrA and the TipF flagellar assembly organizer are expressed.
source: Next, in S-phase, the transcriptional cell cycle activator CtrA and the TipF flagellar assembly organizer are expressed (Huitema et al., 2006; Davis et al., 2013; Quon et al., 1996; Holtzendorff et al., 2004; Fioravanti et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: CtrA induces transcription of early flagellar structural genes and regulators of late flagellar gene expression including the flagellin genes.
source: CtrA induces transcription of early flagellar structural genes and regulators of late flagellar gene expression including the flagellin genes (Quon et al., 1996; Stephens and Shapiro, 1993; Laub et al., 2002; Fumeaux et al., 2014; Fiebig et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Once a functional flagellar secretion structure has been assembled, the newly synthesized flagellins are exported by the FlaF secretion chaperone.
source: Once a functional flagellar secretion structure has been assembled, the newly synthesized flagellins are exported by the FlaF secretion chaperone (Ardissone et al., 2020; Llewellyn et al., 2005; Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and references Figure 1A.

claim: C. crescentus expresses six flagellin paralogs: five structural flagellins (FljKLMNO) and one regulatory flagellin (FljJ).
source: A peculiarity of C. crescentus is that it expresses six flagellin paralogs (Nierman et al., 2001; Faulds-Pain et al., 2011): five structural flagellins (FljKLMNO) each of which is sufficient for flagellar filament formation and motility, while the regulatory FljJ flagellin controls translation of the others (Ardissone et al., 2020) but cannot support filament formation and motility in the absence of other flagellins (Faulds-Pain et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Each of the five structural flagellins (FljKLMNO) is sufficient for flagellar filament formation and motility.
source: A peculiarity of C. crescentus is that it expresses six flagellin paralogs (Nierman et al., 2001; Faulds-Pain et al., 2011): five structural flagellins (FljKLMNO) each of which is sufficient for flagellar filament formation and motility, while the regulatory FljJ flagellin controls translation of the others (Ardissone et al., 2020) but cannot support filament formation and motility in the absence of other flagellins (Faulds-Pain et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The regulatory FljJ flagellin controls translation of the other flagellins.
source: A peculiarity of C. crescentus is that it expresses six flagellin paralogs (Nierman et al., 2001; Faulds-Pain et al., 2011): five structural flagellins (FljKLMNO) each of which is sufficient for flagellar filament formation and motility, while the regulatory FljJ flagellin controls translation of the others (Ardissone et al., 2020) but cannot support filament formation and motility in the absence of other flagellins (Faulds-Pain et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: FljJ cannot support filament formation and motility in the absence of other flagellins.
source: A peculiarity of C. crescentus is that it expresses six flagellin paralogs (Nierman et al., 2001; Faulds-Pain et al., 2011): five structural flagellins (FljKLMNO) each of which is sufficient for flagellar filament formation and motility, while the regulatory FljJ flagellin controls translation of the others (Ardissone et al., 2020) but cannot support filament formation and motility in the absence of other flagellins (Faulds-Pain et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: All six flagellins in C. crescentus are glycosylated in a manner that requires pseudaminic acid as donor.
source: We show that all six flagellins in C. crescentus are glycosylated in a manner that requires pseudaminic acid as donor in a reaction catalyzed by the newly identified soluble OGT FlmG.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The glycosylation of all six flagellins is catalyzed by the newly identified soluble OGT FlmG.
source: We show that all six flagellins in C. crescentus are glycosylated in a manner that requires pseudaminic acid as donor in a reaction catalyzed by the newly identified soluble OGT FlmG.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: FlmG is sufficient for flagellin glycosylation in S. fredii NGR234 that naturally produces pseudaminic acid.
source: Reconstitution of FlmG-dependent flagellin glycosylation in two heterologous systems, S. fredii NGR234 that naturally produces pseudaminic acid to incorporate it into the K-antigen capsule and Escherichia coli K12 cells engineered to produce pseudaminic acid from C. crescentus enzymes, reveals that FlmG is sufficient for flagellin glycosylation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: FlmG is sufficient for flagellin glycosylation in E. coli K12 cells engineered to produce pseudaminic acid from C. crescentus enzymes.
source: Reconstitution of FlmG-dependent flagellin glycosylation in two heterologous systems, S. fredii NGR234 that naturally produces pseudaminic acid to incorporate it into the K-antigen capsule and Escherichia coli K12 cells engineered to produce pseudaminic acid from C. crescentus enzymes, reveals that FlmG is sufficient for flagellin glycosylation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The underlying specificity of glycosylation resides in the modular organization of FlmG: an N-terminal substrate (flagellin) binding domain and a C-terminal glycosyltransferase domain.
source: The underlying specificity of glycosylation resides in the modular organization of FlmG: an N-terminal substrate (flagellin) binding domain and a C-terminal glycosyltransferase domain.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Both domains of FlmG are required for flagellin glycosylation, formation of the flagellar filament, and motility.
source: We show that both domains are required for flagellin glycosylation, formation of the flagellar filament, and motility, but not for flagellin export.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Both domains of FlmG are not required for flagellin export.
source: We show that both domains are required for flagellin glycosylation, formation of the flagellar filament, and motility, but not for flagellin export.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Flagellin glycosylation is tuned with progression of the C. crescentus cell cycle to ensure that glycosylation by FlmG can occur as soon as flagellin is translated.
source: Finally, our studies reveal how flagellin glycosylation is tuned with progression of the C. crescentus cell cycle to ensure that glycosylation by FlmG can occur as soon as flagellin is translated, potentially avoiding competition for flagellin binding by the FlaF secretion chaperone (Figure 1A).

claim: The timing of FlmG accumulation potentially avoids competition for flagellin binding by the FlaF secretion chaperone.
source: Finally, our studies reveal how flagellin glycosylation is tuned with progression of the C. crescentus cell cycle to ensure that glycosylation by FlmG can occur as soon as flagellin is translated, potentially avoiding competition for flagellin binding by the FlaF secretion chaperone (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a potential mechanism and references Figure 1A.

claim: Four C. crescentus transposon mutants each harbor a Tn insertion in the uncharacterized gene CCNA_02961 (neuB).
source: Our previously assembled library of C. crescentus transposon (Tn) motility mutants (Huitema et al., 2006) included four mutants each harboring a Tn insertion in the uncharacterized gene CCNA_02961, predicted to encode a NeuB-like sialic acid synthase (henceforth neuB).

claim: CCNA_02961 (neuB) is predicted to encode a NeuB-like sialic acid synthase.

claim: All four neuB transposon mutants are non-motile on soft agar plates.

claim: All four neuB transposon mutants do not swim when observed by phase contrast light microscopy.
source: All four mutants are non-motile on soft (0.3%) agar plates and do not swim when observed by phase contrast light microscopy.

claim: An in-frame deletion of neuB (ΔneuB) recapitulated the motility defect of the Tn insertions.
source: An in-frame deletion of neuB (ΔneuB) recapitulated the motility defect of the Tn insertions (Figure 1C).

claim: The expression of NeuB from a plasmid corrected the motility defect of ΔneuB cells.

claim: neuB function is required for motility in C. crescentus.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy revealed a flagellar filament on the new pole of WT C. crescentus cells.

claim: ΔneuB cells lack a flagellar filament and only harbor a short protrusion corresponding to a hook structure.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) reveale a flagellar filament on the new pole of WT cells, whereas ΔneuB cells lack a flagellar filament and only harbor a short protrusion corresponding to a hook structure (Figure 1D, see below).

claim: The neuB gene is predicted to encode a 38 kDa protein belonging to the NeuB-family of acetylneuraminate synthases.

claim: Biosynthesis of sugars of the sialic acid family is required for flagellation in C. crescentus.
source: The neuB gene is predicted to encode a 38 kDa protein belonging to the NeuB-family of acetylneuraminate synthases (Vimr et al., 2004; Linton et al., 2000; Chou et al., 2005), suggesting that biosynthesis of sugars of the sialic acid family is required for flagellation in C. crescentus.

evidence: This is stated as an observation from SDS-PAGE analysis.

claim: The reduced molecular mass of flagellin in ΔneuB cells is consistent with NeuB-dependent post-translational modification of flagellin.
source: Moreover, the increased migration of flagellin through SDS-PAGE suggests that the molecular mass is reduced in the absence of NeuB, consistent with NeuB-dependent post-translational modification of flagellin.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the SDS-PAGE results.

claim: FljK expressed in E. coli showed the same mobility as the mobility of FljK in ΔneuB cells.
source: In support of this conclusion, FljK expressed in E. coli showed the same mobility as the mobility of FljK in ΔneuB cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting and references Figure 1F.

claim: All six flagellins show a NeuB-dependent shift in mobility by immunoblotting.
source: Next, we asked whether all six flagellins show a NeuB-dependent shift in mobility by immunoblotting and found this to be the case (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting and references Figure 1G.

claim: Individual flagellins expressed from a plasmid in Δfljx6 cells show a shift to an apparent lower molecular mass in the absence of NeuB.
source: In these experiments, we expressed individual flagellins from a plasmid under the control of an inducible promoter (Pxyl) in cells deleted for all six flagellin genes (Δfljx6) and compared the mobility to that of the flagellin expressed in Δfljx6 ΔneuB cells. In all cases, we observed a shift to an apparent lower molecular mass in the absence of NeuB.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting experiments.

claim: NeuB controls the mobility of all six flagellins.
source: We conclude that NeuB controls the mobility of all six flagellins.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the immunoblotting experiments.

claim: NeuB family members are phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)-dependent synthases that catalyze the condensation of PEP with hexoses to form sialic acid or derivatives, such as pseudaminic acid.
source: NeuB family members are phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)-dependent synthases that catalyze the condensation of PEP with hexoses to form sialic acid or derivatives, such as pseudaminic acid (Vimr et al., 2004; Linton et al., 2000; Sundaram et al., 2004; Chou et al., 2005; Gunawan et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Some bacteria encode more than one NeuB enzyme, for example, the sialic acid synthase NeuB1 and the pseudaminic acid synthase NeuB3 from C. jejuni.
source: Some bacteria encode more than one NeuB enzyme, for example, the sialic acid synthase NeuB1 and the pseudaminic acid synthase NeuB3 from C. jejuni (Linton et al., 2000; Chou et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The Neisseria meningitidis sialic acid synthase NeuB forms a domain-swapped homodimer.
source: The Neisseria meningitidis sialic acid synthase NeuB forms a domain-swapped homodimer, in which each monomer consists of an N-terminal TIM barrel domain similar to other PEP-utilizing enzymes and a C-terminal antifreeze-like domain (Gunawan et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The catalytic site of N. meningitidis NeuB is located in the C-terminal end of the TIM barrel domain.
source: The catalytic site is located in the C-terminal end of the TIM barrel domain, but the antifreeze-like domain from the second monomer in the homodimer contributes key residues required for substrate binding (Gunawan et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The antifreeze-like domain from the second monomer in the N. meningitidis NeuB homodimer contributes key residues required for substrate binding.
source: The catalytic site is located in the C-terminal end of the TIM barrel domain, but the antifreeze-like domain from the second monomer in the homodimer contributes key residues required for substrate binding (Gunawan et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: None of the NeuB variants (E30A, H245A, R322A) were functional in the absence of the inducer vanillate.
source: The expression of NeuB variants from the vanillate-inducible Pvan promoter on pMT335 (Thanbichler et al., 2007) revealed that none of the variants were functional in the absence of the inducer.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from motility and immunoblotting experiments.

claim: All NeuB variants, except H245A, were expressed to comparable steady-state levels in the absence of vanillate.
source: Under these conditions all variants, except H245A, were expressed to comparable steady-state levels as indicated by immunoblotting with polyclonal antibodies to C. crescentus NeuB (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting and references Figure 2C.

claim: In the presence of vanillate, the E30A and R322A NeuB variants showed no activity.
source: In the presence of vanillate, the E30A and R322A variants still showed no activity, whereas H245A exhibited some activity in flagellin modification and motility, albeit far less than WT NeuB, despite accumulating to higher steady-state levels (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from motility and immunoblotting experiments and references Figure 2B and C.

claim: The H245A NeuB variant exhibited some activity in flagellin modification and motility in the presence of vanillate, albeit far less than WT NeuB.
source: In the presence of vanillate, the E30A and R322A variants still showed no activity, whereas H245A exhibited some activity in flagellin modification and motility, albeit far less than WT NeuB, despite accumulating to higher steady-state levels (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from motility and immunoblotting experiments and references Figure 2B and C.

claim: NeuB catalytic activity is required for function in C. crescentus.
source: We conclude that NeuB catalytic activity is required for function in C. crescentus.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the site-directed mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Only C. jejuni NeuB3 can substitute for C. crescentus NeuB in motility assays.
source: Using motility (Figure 3A) and flagellin modification (Figure 3B) as a readout for NeuB activity, we discovered that only NeuB3 can substitute for C. crescentus NeuB, indicating that NeuBCc functions as a pseudaminic acid synthase.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from heterologous complementation experiments and references Figure 3A.

claim: Only C. jejuni NeuB3 can substitute for C. crescentus NeuB in flagellin modification assays.
source: Using motility (Figure 3A) and flagellin modification (Figure 3B) as a readout for NeuB activity, we discovered that only NeuB3 can substitute for C. crescentus NeuB, indicating that NeuBCc functions as a pseudaminic acid synthase.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from heterologous complementation experiments and references Figure 3B.

claim: C. crescentus NeuB functions as a pseudaminic acid synthase.
source: Using motility (Figure 3A) and flagellin modification (Figure 3B) as a readout for NeuB activity, we discovered that only NeuB3 can substitute for C. crescentus NeuB, indicating that NeuBCc functions as a pseudaminic acid synthase.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the heterologous complementation experiments.

claim: S. fredii NGR234 synthetizes a K-antigen capsule composed of pseudaminic acid and glucuronic acid units.
source: We, therefore, turned to the symbiotic alpha-proteobacterium S. fredii NGR234 that synthetizes a K-antigen capsule composed of pseudaminic acid and glucuronic acid units (Le Quéré et al., 2006; Le Quéré and Ghigo, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: S. fredii NeuB (called RkpQ) is encoded in the K-antigen capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis locus (rkp3) on the pNGR234b megaplasmid.
source: S. fredii NeuB (called RkpQ) is encoded in the K-antigen capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis locus (rkp3) on the pNGR234b megaplasmid (Schmeisser et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: S. fredii RkpQ was able to functionally replace NeuB in C. crescentus, restoring motility and flagellin migration to C. crescentus ΔneuB cells.
source: First, we confirmed that S. fredii RkpQ was able to functionally replace NeuB in C. crescentus, restoring motility and flagellin migration to C. crescentus ΔneuB cells (Figure 3A and B), akin to NeuB3 from C. jejuni.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from complementation experiments and references Figure 3A and B.

claim: An rkpQ deletion mutant (ΔrkpQ) in S. fredii blocks synthesis of the K-antigen capsule.
source: To confirm that C. crescentus NeuB is indeed a pseudaminic acid synthase, we constructed an rkpQ deletion mutant (ΔrkpQ) in S. fredii and observed that this mutation blocks synthesis of the K-antigen capsule (Figure 3C), but not motility (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from capsular polysaccharide analysis and references Figure 3C.

claim: An rkpQ deletion mutant (ΔrkpQ) in S. fredii does not affect motility.
source: To confirm that C. crescentus NeuB is indeed a pseudaminic acid synthase, we constructed an rkpQ deletion mutant (ΔrkpQ) in S. fredii and observed that this mutation blocks synthesis of the K-antigen capsule (Figure 3C), but not motility (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from motility assays and references Figure 3D.

claim: Capsule synthesis in S. fredii ΔrkpQ cells was restored by complementation with a plasmid expressing either RkpQ, C. crescentus NeuB or C. jejuni NeuB3.
source: Capsule synthesis was restored by complementation of S. fredii ΔrkpQ cells with a plasmid expressing either RkpQ, C. crescentus NeuB or C. jejuni NeuB3.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from capsular polysaccharide analysis.

claim: C. jejuni NeuB1 and NeuB2 could not restore capsular polysaccharide production in S. fredii ΔrkpQ cells.
source: By contrast, C. jejuni NeuB1 and NeuB2 could not restore capsular polysaccharide production (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from capsular polysaccharide analysis and references Figure 3C.

claim: Pseudaminic acid synthesis is required for motility and flagellin modification in C. crescentus.
source: Thus, pseudaminic acid synthesis is required for motility and flagellin modification in C. crescentus and pseudaminic acid synthases are interchangeable.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the heterologous complementation experiments.

claim: Pseudaminic acid synthases are interchangeable.
source: Thus, pseudaminic acid synthesis is required for motility and flagellin modification in C. crescentus and pseudaminic acid synthases are interchangeable.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the heterologous complementation experiments.

claim: Ten transposon mutants have a Tn insertion in the CCNA_01524 (flmG) gene.
source: Inspection of the Tn insertion sites revealed 10 mutants with a Tn insertion in the CCNA_01524 (henceforth flmG) gene: six bear a himar1 Tn insertion at different positions in flmG (strains NS25, NS55, NS81, NS128, NS157, and NS192), while an Ez-Tn5 insertion disrupts flmG in four other mutants (NS149, NS211, NS322, and NS327).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the transposon library.

claim: The flmG gene had previously been implicated in motility and flagellin biosynthesis.
source: The flmG gene had previously been implicated in motility and flagellin biosynthesis (Leclerc et al., 1998; Schoenlein et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1993; Schoenlein and Ely, 1989; Schoenlein et al., 1989) and is predicted to encode a 596-residue protein of 65 kDa containing an N-terminal domain (NTD) with tetratricopeptide (TPR) repeats, known to be involved in protein-protein interactions, and a C-terminal domain (CTD) resembling glycosyltransferases (GT-B superfamily).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: flmG is predicted to encode a 596-residue protein of 65 kDa containing an N-terminal domain (NTD) with tetratricopeptide (TPR) repeats and a C-terminal domain (CTD) resembling glycosyltransferases (GT-B superfamily).
source: The flmG gene had previously been implicated in motility and flagellin biosynthesis (Leclerc et al., 1998; Schoenlein et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1993; Schoenlein and Ely, 1989; Schoenlein et al., 1989) and is predicted to encode a 596-residue protein of 65 kDa containing an N-terminal domain (NTD) with tetratricopeptide (TPR) repeats, known to be involved in protein-protein interactions, and a C-terminal domain (CTD) resembling glycosyltransferases (GT-B superfamily).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on sequence analysis.

claim: Tetratricopeptide (TPR) repeats are known to be involved in protein-protein interactions.
source: The flmG gene had previously been implicated in motility and flagellin biosynthesis (Leclerc et al., 1998; Schoenlein et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1993; Schoenlein and Ely, 1989; Schoenlein et al., 1989) and is predicted to encode a 596-residue protein of 65 kDa containing an N-terminal domain (NTD) with tetratricopeptide (TPR) repeats, known to be involved in protein-protein interactions, and a C-terminal domain (CTD) resembling glycosyltransferases (GT-B superfamily).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: An in-frame deletion in flmG (ΔflmG) results in a defect in motility.
source: We constructed an in-frame deletion in flmG (ΔflmG) and found the resulting mutant cells have a defect in motility (Figure 4A) and flagellin modification (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from motility assays and references Figure 4A.

claim: An in-frame deletion in flmG (ΔflmG) results in a defect in flagellin modification.
source: We constructed an in-frame deletion in flmG (ΔflmG) and found the resulting mutant cells have a defect in motility (Figure 4A) and flagellin modification (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting and references Figure 4B.

claim: The motility and flagellin modification defects of ΔflmG cells were corrected by the expression of FlmG in trans from Pvan on pMT335.
source: The motility and flagellin modification defects were corrected by the expression of FlmG in trans from Pvan on pMT335 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from complementation experiments and references Figure 4A and B.

claim: FlmG acts in the same pathway as NeuB as predicted for an OGT responsible for the post-translational O-glycosylation of flagellins in C. crescentus.
source: Thus, FlmG acts in the same pathway as NeuB as predicted for an OGT responsible for the post-translational O-glycosylation of flagellins in C. crescentus.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic experiments.

claim: When FljK is expressed alone in WT S. fredii, it migrates faster, like in the C. crescentus ΔneuB mutant.
source: In the absence of FlmG, FljK showed the same mobility on SDS-PAGE as in C. crescentus ΔneuB cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting experiments.

claim: Co-expression of FlmG and FljK in S. fredii results in a shift in the migration profile of FljK, similar to that observed in C. crescentus WT cells.
source: However, upon co-expression of FlmG, FljK shifted to a species with higher molecular mass and identical apparent migration on SDS-PAGE to that observed for FljK in C. crescentus WT cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting experiments.

claim: The shift in FljK migration upon co-expression with FlmG in S. fredii was dependent on the presence of pseudaminic acid.
source: Importantly, this shift was dependent on the presence of pseudaminic acid, since FljK co-expressed with FlmG in S. fredii cells lacking pseudaminic acid (ΔrkpQ or Δrkp3_013, see below) had the same mobility by SDS-PAGE as FljK expressed in C. crescentus ΔneuB or ΔflmG cells, or in WT S. fredii cells without FlmG (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting experiments and references Figure 4C.

claim: FlmG is required and sufficient for flagellin modification in the presence of pseudaminic acid.
source: We conclude that FlmG is required and sufficient for flagellin modification in the presence of pseudaminic acid.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the heterologous expression experiments.

claim: The expression of the FlmG CTD alone did not restore motility or flagellin modification to C. crescentus ΔflmG cells.
source: Indeed, the expression of the CTD alone did not restore motility or flagellin modification to C. crescentus ΔflmG cells (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from motility and immunoblotting experiments and references Figure 4A and D.

claim: A strong interaction was observed between each of the flagellins (FljJ, FljK, and FljM) and the FlmG NTD (TPR) in BACTH assays.
source: Notably, a strong interaction was observed between each of the flagellins and the FlmG NTD (TPR), but not FlmG CTD (GT, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from BACTH assays and references Figure 4E.

claim: No interaction was observed between the flagellins and the FlmG CTD (GT) in BACTH assays.
source: Notably, a strong interaction was observed between each of the flagellins and the FlmG NTD (TPR), but not FlmG CTD (GT, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from BACTH assays and references Figure 4E.

claim: The TPR-containing NTD of FlmG is required and sufficient for a specific interaction with multiple flagellins.
source: These BACTH results along with the domain analysis show the TPR-containing NTD is required and sufficient for a specific interaction of FlmG with multiple flagellins performing structural or regulatory functions, consistent with our finding that all flagellins are modified with pseudaminic acid by FlmG (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from BACTH assays and domain analysis and references Figure 1G.

claim: The flmD and flmC transcripts do not fluctuate substantially in abundance during the cell cycle.
source: We noted that while the flmD and flmC transcripts do not fluctuate substantially in abundance during the cell cycle (Schrader et al., 2016), the flmGH and flmAB transcripts peak in abundance during the early pre-divisional cell stage (90 min into the cell cycle, Figure 6A), while the neuB transcript is most abundant at the late pre-divisional cell stage (after 120 min, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from RNA-Seq and Ribo-Seq analysis and references Figure 6A.

claim: The flmGH and flmAB transcripts peak in abundance during the early pre-divisional cell stage (90 min into the cell cycle).
source: We noted that while the flmD and flmC transcripts do not fluctuate substantially in abundance during the cell cycle (Schrader et al., 2016), the flmGH and flmAB transcripts peak in abundance during the early pre-divisional cell stage (90 min into the cell cycle, Figure 6A), while the neuB transcript is most abundant at the late pre-divisional cell stage (after 120 min, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from RNA-Seq and Ribo-Seq analysis and references Figure 6A.

claim: The neuB transcript is most abundant at the late pre-divisional cell stage (after 120 min).
source: We noted that while the flmD and flmC transcripts do not fluctuate substantially in abundance during the cell cycle (Schrader et al., 2016), the flmGH and flmAB transcripts peak in abundance during the early pre-divisional cell stage (90 min into the cell cycle, Figure 6A), while the neuB transcript is most abundant at the late pre-divisional cell stage (after 120 min, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from RNA-Seq and Ribo-Seq analysis and references Figure 6A.

claim: Previous ChIP-Seq studies revealed that the essential cell cycle regulator CtrA binds to the predicted promoter region of flmG, flmA, and neuB.
source: Previous chromatin-immunoprecipitation deep-sequencing (ChIP-Seq) studies revealed that the essential cell cycle regulator CtrA binds to the predicted promoter region of flmG, flmA, and neuB (Fumeaux et al., 2014; Fiebig et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: At the permissive temperature (30°C), ctrA401 cells show substantially reduced activity of the promoter probe reporters of flmG, flmA, and neuB.
source: We observed a similar reduction in activity of the promoter probe reporters of flmG, flmA, and neuB in ctrA401 cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from β-galactosidase assays and references Figure 6B.

claim: A gain-of-function mutation in ctrA (ctrA*, encoding the T170A substitution) increases the activity of the flmG, flmA, and neuB promoter reporters compared to the isogenic parent.
source: Conversely, a gain-of-function mutation in ctrA (ctrA*, encoding the T170A substitution) increases the activity of these reporters compared to the isogenic parent (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from β-galactosidase assays and references Figure 6B.

claim: Transcription of flmG, flmA, and neuB is directly integrated into the cell cycle via CtrA.
source: Thus, transcription of flmG, flmA, and neuB is directly integrated into the cell cycle via CtrA, as is the case for the other flagellar genes that are CtrA-dependent (directly or indirectly), including the FlaF flagellin secretion chaperone that binds all six flagellins (Ardissone et al., 2020) to direct their secretion and that accumulates in dividing cells (Fumeaux et al., 2014; Llewellyn et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the promoter probe experiments and supported by citations.

claim: Immunoblotting of extracts from synchronized cells did not reveal substantial changes in abundance of NeuB during the C. crescentus cell cycle.
source: Immunoblotting of extracts from synchronized cells harvested at different times during the cell cycle probed with antibodies to FlmG and NeuB did not reveal substantial changes in abundance of NeuB during the C. crescentus cell cycle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting and references Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The levels of FlmG increased steadily, peaking at the end of the cell cycle.
source: However, the levels of FlmG increased steadily, peaking at the end of the cell cycle (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting and references Figure 6C.

claim: FlmG is already abundant before cell division, while the FlaF secretion chaperone accumulates in dividing cells.
source: Because FlmG is already abundant before cell division, while the FlaF secretion chaperone accumulates in dividing cells (Llewellyn et al., 2005), flagellin modification by FlmG can occur before the FlaF-dependent secretion and potentially avoids competition between FlmG and FlaF for flagellins.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and interpretation from immunoblotting and supported by a citation.

claim: Flagellin modification by FlmG can occur before the FlaF-dependent secretion.
source: Because FlmG is already abundant before cell division, while the FlaF secretion chaperone accumulates in dividing cells (Llewellyn et al., 2005), flagellin modification by FlmG can occur before the FlaF-dependent secretion and potentially avoids competition between FlmG and FlaF for flagellins.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation from the temporal accumulation data.

claim: The temporal accumulation of FlmG potentially avoids competition between FlmG and FlaF for flagellins.
source: Because FlmG is already abundant before cell division, while the FlaF secretion chaperone accumulates in dividing cells (Llewellyn et al., 2005), flagellin modification by FlmG can occur before the FlaF-dependent secretion and potentially avoids competition between FlmG and FlaF for flagellins.
evidence: This is stated as a potential mechanism based on the temporal accumulation data.

claim: The Maf glycosyltransferase from Geobacillus kaustophilus and Clostridium botulinum can modify flagellin with N-acetylneuraminic acid or 3-deoxy-D-manno-octulosonic acid by O-linkage at threonine and serine residues when expressed in E. coli.
source: Recently evidence was provided that the Maf glycosyltransferase from Geobacillus kaustophilus and Clostridium botulinum can modify flagellin with N-acetylneuraminic acid or 3-deoxy-D-manno-octulosonic acid by O-linkage at threonine and serine residues when expressed in E. coli (Khairnar et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The Maf orthologs from Aeromonas caviae and Magnetospirillum magneticum magneticum are required for flagellin glycosylation in vivo.
source: The Maf orthologs from Aeromonas caviae and Magnetospirillum magneticum magneticum are required for flagellin glycosylation in vivo (Sulzenbacher et al., 2018; Parker et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: C. crescentus does not encode a Maf ortholog in its genome.
source: While C. crescentus does not encode a Maf ortholog in its genome, we discovered that it uses FlmG, the defining member of a hitherto unknown class of OGTs, to glycosylate flagellins in hosts that can synthesize pseudaminic acid.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from genome analysis.

claim: C. crescentus modifies the FljK flagellin at four threonine residues with a molecule predicted to be an O-linked glycan.
source: The very recent evidence that C. crescentus modifies the FljK flagellin at four threonine residues with a molecule predicted to be an O-linked glycan (Montemayor et al., 2020) aligns well with our finding that pseudaminic acid is required for FlmG to modify FljK.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The demonstration that FlmG glycosylates flagellin in E. coli expressing a synthetic pseudaminic acid biosynthesis (flm) operon from C. crescentus simplifies future analyses of the donor promiscuity for FlmG-dependent flagellin glycosylation.
source: Our demonstration that FlmG glycosylates flagellin in E. coli expressing a synthetic pseudaminic acid biosynthesis (flm) operon from C. crescentus simplifies future analyses of the donor promiscuity for FlmG-dependent flagellin glycosylation, as it can now be simply achieved by the expression of orthologous sialic acid biosynthesis pathways in E. coli.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the implications of the study.

claim: Since all six C. crescentus flagellins are glycosylated by FlmG, a certain degree of substrate promiscuity is inherent in the system.
source: Since all six C. crescentus flagellins are glycosylated by FlmG, a certain degree of substrate promiscuity is inherent in the system.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: There are at least 20 serine and threonine residues that are conserved between FljJ and FljK that FlmG could potentially modify.
source: While the FljJ flagellin only bears 49% amino acid identity compared to the other flagellins, there are still at least 20 serine and threonine residues that are conserved between FljJ and FljK and that FlmG could potentially modify.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from sequence analysis.

claim: Only one of the four threonines that are modified in FljK is present in all six flagellins.
source: However, only one of the four threonines that are modified in FljK is present in all six flagellins (Montemayor et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The FlmG NTD binds the flagellins via the TPR region and this domain is required for motility and efficient glycosylation.
source: We showed that the FlmG NTD binds the flagellins via the TPR region and that this domain is required for motility and efficient glycosylation (Figure 4A, D and E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study and references Figure 4A, D and E.

claim: A free-floating glycosyltransferase (CTD) in the cytoplasm cannot bind the flagellins alone in BACTH assays.
source: A free-floating glycosyltransferase (CTD) in the cytoplasm cannot bind the flagellins alone in BACTH assays (Figure 4E) and can not modify sufficient flagellin to support assembly of the flagellar filament in C. crescentus.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from BACTH assays and references Figure 4E.

claim: A free-floating glycosyltransferase (CTD) in the cytoplasm cannot modify sufficient flagellin to support assembly of the flagellar filament in C. crescentus.
source: A free-floating glycosyltransferase (CTD) in the cytoplasm cannot bind the flagellins alone in BACTH assays (Figure 4E) and can not modify sufficient flagellin to support assembly of the flagellar filament in C. crescentus.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from motility assays.

claim: Recent BACTH assays revealed that the FlaF secretion chaperone binds the six flagellins.
source: Recent BACTH assays revealed that the FlaF secretion chaperone binds the six flagellins as well (Ardissone et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: All flagellins are assembled into the flagellar filament.
source: While all flagellins are assembled into the flagellar filament (Driks et al., 1989), FljJ is the only flagellin that cannot assemble into a flagellar filament on its own (Faulds-Pain et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: FljJ is the first flagellin to be synthesized and exported during the cell cycle as its location within the filament is the most proximal to the hook.
source: FljJ is the first flagellin to be synthesized and exported during the cell cycle as its location within the filament is the most proximal to the hook (Driks et al., 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: As an exported flagellin, FljJ is also glycosylated like the other flagellins and it therefore must also be bound by FlmG and FlaF.
source: As an exported flagellin, FljJ is also glycosylated like the other flagellins and it therefore must also be bound by FlmG and FlaF (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the findings and references Figure 1A.

claim: FlmG and FlaF could potentially compete for the same substrate.
source: Therefore, FlmG and FlaF could potentially compete for the same substrate.
evidence: This is stated as a potential scenario based on the findings.

claim: FlmG is already present well before FlaF accumulates.
source: However, FlmG is already present well before FlaF accumulates (Llewellyn et al., 2005; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting and references Figure 6C and a citation.

claim: Flagellin modification does occur in mutants lacking a flagellar hook basal body complex.
source: Moreover, flagellin modification does occur in mutants lacking a flagellar hook basal body complex (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C) or the flagellin chaperone FlaF (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), confirming that modification can occur without the secretion apparatus and the secretion chaperone.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from immunoblotting and references Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Flagellin modification does occur in mutants lacking the flagellin chaperone FlaF.
source: Moreover, flagellin modification does occur in mutants lacking a flagellar hook basal body complex (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C) or the flagellin chaperone FlaF (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), confirming that modification can occur without the secretion apparatus and the secretion chaperone.
